Barack Obama (born August 4, 1961) is an American politician who served as the 44th president of the United States from 2009 to 2017.

Bob Hawke (9 December 1929 - 16 May 2019) was an Australian politician, trade unionist, economist and central banker who served as the 23rd prime minister of Australia from 1983 to 1991.

Cesar Chavez (Latin American; March 31, 1927 - April 23, 1993) was an American labor unionist and political activist.
Born in a Tennessee log cabin, which Democrat served nearly twelve years as U.S. secretary of state under Franklin Roosevelt — the longest tenure in that office's history?

Cordell Hull (October 2, 1871 - July 23, 1955) was an American politician and diplomat who served as the United States secretary of state for nearly twelve years under President Franklin D. Roosevelt.
Born to a low-status family in the Roman province of Dalmatia, this Roman emperor rose through the military ranks before becoming one of the few to voluntarily abdicate. Who is he?
Diocletian (Ancient; 242/245 - 311/312), nicknamed Jovius, was Roman emperor from 284 until his abdication in 305.
A longtime ally of Robert Mugabe and his first vice-president, this politician was dismissed only to seize power in a 2017 coup and has led Zimbabwe ever since — who is he?
Emmerson Mnangagwa (born 15 September 1942) is a Zimbabwean politician who has served as the president of Zimbabwe since 2017.

Founded by a beloved Italian saint known for his devotion to poverty and nature, this Catholic religious family includes three orders for men and one for women, the Order of Saint Clare — what movement is it called?
Franciscans are a group of related organizations in the Catholic Church, founded by the Italian saint Francis of Assisi.
This Israeli soldier was captured by Palestinian militants in a 2006 cross-border tunnel raid and held by Hamas for more than five years before his release in a 2011 prisoner exchange — who is he?
Gilad Shalit (born 28 August 1986) is an Israeli former soldier who, on 25 June 2006, was captured by Palestinian militants in a cross-border raid via tunnels near the Israeli border.
This former ruler of a Gulf nation seized power from his own father in a bloodless 1995 coup and presided over the country's natural gas boom until abdicating in 2013 — who is he?
Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani (1 January 1952 - 12 July 2026) was Emir of Qatar from 1995 until his abdication in 2013.
Three former PayPal employees launched this video platform in 2005 with the slogan "Broadcast Yourself" before Google bought it for $1.65 billion — which topic's chronicle is this?

History of YouTube is an American online video-sharing platform headquartered in San Bruno, California, founded by three former PayPal employees - Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, and Jawed Karim - in February 2005.
Serving as Japan's prime minister from 1931, this elder statesman was assassinated in office in 1932 at age 76 — who was he?
Inukai Tsuyoshi was a Japanese statesman who served as prime minister of Japan from 1931 to his assassination in 1932.
Generally hailed as the first major investment banker in the United States, he helped finance the Union war effort and then the postwar push of railroads into the Northwest — who was he?

Jay Cooke (August 10, 1821 - February 16, 1905) was an American financier who helped finance the Union war effort during the American Civil War and the postwar development of railroads in the northwestern United States.
A former Tasmanian schoolteacher who served as premier of his state, this man crossed from Labor to lead the new United Australia Party and became prime minister, dying in office in 1939. Who was he?
Joseph Lyons (15 September 1879 - 7 April 1939) was an Australian politician who served as the tenth prime minister of Australia, from 1932 until his death in 1939.

Rising to Turkey's presidency after leading the 1980 military coup, this military officer served as the country's 7th president from 1982 to 1989 and was later sentenced to life imprisonment for the coup — who was he?
Kenan Evren (17 July 1917 - 9 May 2015) was a Turkish military officer who served as the 7th president of Turkey from 1982 to 1989.
This New Testament figure was restored to life by Jesus four days after his death, an event recounted in the Gospel of John and venerated in Eastern Orthodoxy as 'the Four-Days Dead' — who is he?
Lazarus of Bethany is a figure of the New Testament whose life is restored by Jesus four days after his death, as told in the Gospel of John.
Born in Warsaw in 1969, this Polish politician held the Interior Ministry's Secretary of State post from 2019 to 2023 and lost his parliamentary seat after being convicted of a crime — who is he?

Born Qajar-Azodanlu in 1953, which Iranian dissident politician leads the National Council of Resistance of Iran, an organization seeking to overthrow Iran's government?

Maryam Rajavi (born 4 December 1953) is an Iranian dissident politician who currently serves as president of the National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI), an organization advocating the overthrow of the Iranian government.
Nicknamed 'the Red Napoleon,' this Soviet military theorist and general was executed in the Moscow trials of the 1930s — who is he?
Mikhail Tukhachevsky was Russian and Soviet military leader (1893–1937).
Captured during an intelligence mission in New York and executed by the British in 1776, this Continental Army officer was named Connecticut's state hero in 1985 — who is he?
Nathan Hale (June 6, 1755 - September 22, 1776) was an American Patriot, soldier, and spy for the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War.
Before becoming Germany's chancellor in 2021, this Social Democrat served as Angela Merkel's vice chancellor and finance minister, and earlier as First Mayor of Hamburg — who is he?
Olaf Scholz (born 14 June 1958) is a German politician who served as the chancellor of Germany from 2021 to 2025.
The daughter of a Spartan king, this legendary queen of Ithaca stayed faithful to her husband Odysseus for years, cleverly outwitting more than a hundred suitors while he was away. Who is she?
Penelope (p-; Ancient) is a legendary mythological Greek Queen of Ithaca and Princess of Sparta, who plays a prominent character in Homer's Odyssey.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses, this legendary Cypriot sculptor falls hopelessly in love with a statue of his own making — who is he?
Pygmalion (mythology) (Ancient) was a legendary figure of Cyprus.

Rising from general to Tsar of the First Bulgarian Empire, this ruler spent his reign in near-constant war defending his country's independence against Byzantine emperor Basil II until his death in 1014 — who was he?
Samuel of Bulgaria (also Samoil or Samuil; Old Church Slavonic: Самоилъ; died 6 October 1014) was the Tsar (Emperor) of the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 6 October 1014.
This Italian media tycoon served three stints as prime minister and, at his death in 2023, was worth $6.8 billion — making him the 352nd-richest man in the world — who was he?

Silvio Berlusconi (29 September 1936 - 12 June 2023) was an Italian media tycoon and politician who served as the prime minister of Italy in three governments from 1994 to 1995, 2001 to 2006 and 2008 to 2011.
Starting out as a Muslim League youth worker in British India, he went on to lead the first government of Bangladesh as its wartime prime minister during the 1971 independence struggle — who was he?
Tajuddin Ahmad (23 July 1925 - 3 November 1975) was a Bangladeshi politician.

Constantine IX Monomachos: Byzantine emperor from 1042 to 1055.

David Ben-Gurion: Prime Minister of Israel (1948–1953; 1955–1963)

Dito Ariotedjo: Indonesian businessman and politician.

Leonid Kuchma: President of Ukraine from 1994 to 2005. Kuchma took office after winning the 1994 presidential election against his rival, incumbent President Leonid Kravchuk.

Louis XIII: King of France from 1610 to 1643.

Malayan Emergency: 1948–1960 British colonial war in Malaya. The communists gained support from many civilians, mainly those from the Chinese community.

Klinefelter syndrome (KS), also known as 47,XXY, is a chromosome anomaly.
Bash (Unix shell): Brian Fox. Bash (short for "Bourne Again SHell") is an interactive command interpreter and command language developed for Unix-like operating systems.
Airbus A220: Bombardier Aerospace. The Airbus A220 is a family of five-abreast narrow-body airliners by Airbus Canada Limited Partnership (ACLP).
Cannoli: Italy. Cannoli are Sicilian pastries consisting of a tube-shaped shell of fried pastry dough, filled with a sweet and creamy filling containing ricotta cheese.
Who is credited with discovering Copernicium?
GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
Copernicium: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cn and atomic number 112.
Who is credited with discovering Pluto?
Pluto: Clyde Tombaugh. Pluto (minor-planet number 134340) is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Who is credited with discovering Influenza A virus?
Influenza A virus: Christopher Andrewes. Influenza A virus, or IAV, is a pathogen with strains that cause seasonal flu in humans; it can also infect birds and some mammals.
Heading Switzerland's Federal Department of Home Affairs for over a decade, this politician succeeded Marija Pejčinović Burić atop a major European institution in 2024 — who is he?
Alain Berset (French; born 9 April 1972) is a Swiss politician who served as a Member of the Swiss Federal Council from 2012 to 2023.
Struck off the medical register for the fraudulent 1998 Lancet paper that falsely tied the MMR vaccine to autism, this former surgeon sparked a plunge in vaccination rates — who is he?
Andrew Wakefield (born 3 September 1956) is an English fraudster, anti-vaccine activist, and former senior surgeon.
This mid-sized zodiac constellation, sitting between Pisces and Taurus, has represented a ram since late Babylonian times — though its stars once formed a farmhand. Which one is it?
Aries (constellation) is one of the constellations of the zodiac. It is located in the Northern celestial hemisphere between Pisces to the west and Taurus to the east.
Nicknamed 'Red-Stockings,' this French herding dog breed hails from the plains of Central France — which breed is it?
Beauceron (French) is a herding dog breed originating from the plains of Central France.
Composed mostly of plasma along with red cells, white cells, and platelets, this body fluid ferries oxygen and nutrients to cells while hauling waste away — name the fluid?

Blood is a body fluid in the circulatory system of humans and other vertebrates that delivers necessary substances such as nutrients and oxygen to the cells of the body, and transports metabolic waste products away from those same cells.

This opioid medication used to treat addiction and pain can be delivered under the tongue, through the cheek, by injection, patch, or implant — and is often combined with naloxone to deter misuse — what drug is it?
Buprenorphine is an opioid used to treat opioid use disorder, acute pain, and chronic pain.
Named for its habit of burrowing nests into dead wood or bamboo, this genus of some 500 bee species includes one soil-tunneling exception among its 31 subgenera — what insect is it?
Carpenter bee are species in the genus Xylocopa of the subfamily Xylocopinae.
Originating in Northern China, this spitz-type dog breed is known for a dense double coat that forms a distinctive ruff around the neck — name the breed?
Chow Chow is a spitz-type of dog breed originally from Northern China.
Scholars still argue whether it merely transmits meaning or also creates it, but the simplest definition of this concept is the transmission of information — what is it?
Communication is commonly defined as the transmission of information.
Native to Mexico and Central America and related to the sunflower and daisy, this genus of 49 tuberous perennial species blooms in nearly every color except blue — which genus?
Dahlia is a genus of bushy, tuberous, herbaceous perennial plants native to Mexico and Central America.
A member of the catecholamine family made by stripping a carboxyl group from L-DOPA, this brain chemical is central to reward-motivated behavior — what is it?
Dopamine (DA, a contraction of 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine) is a neuromodulatory molecule that plays several important roles in cells.
Not a single disease but a syndrome of overall brain dysfunction with many possible causes, this term's Greek roots literally mean 'brain suffering' — what is it called?
Encephalopathy (from Ancient Greek (enkphalos) 'brain' and (pthos) 'suffering') is any disorder or disease of the brain, especially chronic degenerative conditions.
What is the scientific term for the solid waste material left after digestion, discharged through the anus, and sometimes reused as fertilizer, fuel, or building material?
Feces (also faeces or fces or poop) are the solid or semi-solid remains of food that was not digested in the small intestine, and has been broken down by bacteria in the large intestine.
This Austrian-school economist shared the 1974 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Gunnar Myrdal for work on how prices communicate information — who is he?
Friedrich Hayek (8 May 1899 - 23 March 1992) was an Austrian economist and philosopher.
One of Europe's smallest songbirds, this kinglet sports a bright orange-and-yellow crest in males and closely resembles the firecrest — which bird?
Goldcrest (Regulus regulus) is a very small passerine bird in the kinglet family.
This daisy-family genus native to North America and Mexico includes the common sunflower and the Jerusalem artichoke among its roughly 50 species — which genus?
Helianthus is a genus comprising around 50 species of annual and perennial flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae commonly known as sunflowers.
With atomic number 1, this element's most common isotope holds just one proton and one electron, and it's what stars like the Sun mainly burn — what is it?
Hydrogen is a chemical element; it has the symbol H and atomic number 1.
Its name comes from the Ancient Greek for 'violet,' fitting for an element that boils into a violet gas — and it sits at atomic number 53 as the heaviest stable halogen. What is it?
Iodine is a chemical element; it has symbol I and atomic number 53.
Two years after unveiling the first mechanical television system, this Scottish engineer achieved the first-ever transatlantic television transmission in 1928 — who is he?
John Logie Baird (13 August 1888 - 14 June 1946) was a Scottish inventor, electrical engineer and innovator who demonstrated the world's first mechanical television system on 26 January 1926.
Striking children as they wean, up to about age five, this protein-deficiency disorder produces edema and a fatty, enlarged liver — what is it called?
Kwashiorkor (-kr) is a form of severe protein malnutrition characterized by edema and an enlarged liver with fatty infiltrates.
Popular in aquariums but a destructive invader in the Atlantic and Mediterranean, this venomous Indo-Pacific creature warns predators off with bold red and black stripes — what is it?
Lionfish (genus Pterois) are venomous marine fish native to the Indo-Pacific.
Domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from wild teosinte, this grain was grown by Native Americans alongside beans and squash in the 'Three Sisters' method — name the tall grass crop?
Maize (Zea mays), also known as corn, is a tall stout grass that produces cereal grain.
Triggered by falling progesterone, this monthly discharge from the uterine lining signals that pregnancy hasn't occurred and typically first arrives at "menarche" between ages 11 and 13 — what is it?
Menstruation (also known as a period, among other colloquial terms) is the regular discharge of blood and mucosal tissue from the inner lining of the uterus through the vagina.
Also called a mutt, this designation covers any dog outside official breed standards — with an estimated 150 million examples worldwide, believed to enjoy 'hybrid vigor' — what's it called?
Mongrel is any dog which does not belong to one officially recognized breed.
This silvery lanthanide, found in the minerals monazite and bastnäsite, is about as common as cobalt or nickel despite its 'rare earth' label — which element?
Neodymium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nd and atomic number 60.
This Persian polymath and poet was the first to provide a general geometric solution to all third-degree polynomial equations, using the intersection of conic sections. Who is he?
Omar Khayyam (1048-1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.
Designed by Niklaus Wirth to encourage structured programming and named after a French mathematician-philosopher, this language was developed in the pattern of ALGOL 60 — name it?

Pascal (programming language) is an imperative and procedural programming language, designed by Niklaus Wirth as a small, efficient language intended to encourage good programming practices using structured programming and data structuring.
Its name comes from the Greek for 'love of wisdom,' and physics and psychology were once branches of it — what is this rational inquiry into existence and knowledge?

Philosophy (from Ancient Greek philosophia, lit. 'love of wisdom') is a systematic study of general and fundamental questions concerning topics like existence, knowledge, mind, reason, language, and value.
Abundant throughout the plant kingdom, this broad class of naturally occurring phenolic compounds includes flavonoids and ellagitannin — what is the family called?
Polyphenol are a large family of naturally occurring phenols.
Which industry has expanded from traditional books and newspapers to e-books, websites, and video games, with giants like Thomson Reuters and News Corp among its biggest players?
Publishing is the process of making information, literature, music, software, and other content, whether in physical or digital form, available to the public for sale or free of charge.
This positive-sense RNA virus in the Enterovirus genus is the most common viral infectious agent in humans and the leading cause of the common cold — name the virus?
Rhinovirus (from the Ancient) is a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the genus Enterovirus in the family Picornaviridae.
This Harvard political scientist argued in a 1993 theory that future conflict would erupt not between countries but between cultures — a 'clash of civilizations.' Who was he?
Samuel P. Huntington (April 18, 1927 - December 24, 2008) was an American political scientist, adviser, and academic.

This medical state of insufficient blood flow to body tissues comes in four main types, from hypovolemic to cardiogenic, and can progress from weakness and rapid breathing to confusion or cardiac arrest. What is this condition called?
Shock (circulatory) is the state of insufficient blood flow to the tissues of the body as a result of problems with the circulatory system.
First described in 1780, this slender, long-legged antelope of southern Africa wears a white face crossed by a dark stripe from eye to mouth — and both sexes sport backward-curving horns. What is it?
Springbok (Antidorcas marsupialis) is an antelope found mainly in south and southwest Africa.

This genus of about a dozen woody flowering shrubs in the olive family, native from southeastern Europe to East Asia, is closely related to privet and provides food for several moth larvae — what is it commonly called?
Syringa is a genus of 12 currently recognized species of flowering woody plants in the olive family called lilacs.
This genus of roughly 350 species of aromatic Mediterranean herbs is the source of a common culinary seasoning that shares its name — what is the genus?
Thymus (plant) (thymes) contains about 350 species of aromatic perennial herbaceous plants and subshrubs in the family Lamiaceae.
Named from the Greek word for 'cheese' after being first isolated from milk protein in 1846, this standard amino acid is more water-loving than its close relative phenylalanine. Name the amino acid?
Tyrosine (symbol Tyr or Y) or 4-hydroxyphenylalanine is one of the 20 standard amino acids that are used by cells to synthesize proteins.
The largest bird of prey on the Australian continent, distinguished by long broad wings, fully feathered legs, and an unmistakable wedge-shaped tail. What is it?
Wedge-tailed eagle (Aquila audax) is the largest bird of prey in the continent of Australia.
Also known as the empirical guideline, this statistical shorthand describes the percentage of values within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean in a normal distribution — which one?
Transmitted by the bite of an infected tsetse fly, this parasitic infection caused by Trypanosoma brucei is better known in humans as 'sleeping sickness' — what's its formal name?
African trypanosomiasis: Parasitic disease also known as sleeping sickness.
With more than 1,100 species including onions, garlic, leeks, and chives, this is the largest genus in the flowering plant family Amaryllidaceae — which genus?
Allium: Genus of flowering plants. The flowers form an umbel at the top of a leafless stalk.
This Russian physicist miraculously survived a 1978 accident in which a high-energy proton beam from a particle accelerator passed directly through his skull — who is he?
Anatoli Bugorski: Soviet and Russian scientist (born 1942)
Commonly called a canker sore, this recurring condition produces benign mouth ulcers that heal within 7 to 10 days but often return three to six times a year — what is it?
Aphthous stomatitis: Common oral condition lasting 7–10 days.
One of the oldest of the natural sciences, it leans on math, physics, and chemistry to explain everything from comets to quasars beyond Earth's atmosphere — what field is this?
Astronomy: Scientific study of celestial objects.
Originating in Central Africa, this hunting dog breed doesn't bark but makes an unusual yodel-like sound instead, earning it a nickname — what breed is it?
Basenji: Central African breed of dog. The Fédération Cynologique Internationale places it in the Spitz and "primitive types" categories, while the American Kennel Club classifies it as a hound.

Named after two French physicists who discovered it in 1820, this equation in magnetostatics relates a magnetic field to the strength, direction, and distance of an electric current — which physics rule?
Biot–Savart law: Law of classical electromagnetism.
Holding the title of smallest great ape, this creature has pinker lips and a darker face than its close cousin, and was once dismissed as merely a 'pygmy' subspecies of it — what is it?
Bonobo: Species of great ape. Taxonomically, members of the chimpanzee/bonobo subtribe Panina—composed entirely by the genus Pan—are collectively termed panins.
Nicknamed 'the lawyer' and 'freshwater cod,' this coldwater fish is the only member of its genus and the sole freshwater species in its entire order — what fish is it?
Burbot: Species of fish. The species is closely related to marine fish such as the common ling and cusk, all of which belong to the family Lotidae (rocklings).
Its Latin name means 'horned goat,' and it's often pictured as a half-goat, half-fish sea creature — which is the smallest constellation of the zodiac?
Capricornus: Zodiac constellation in the southern hemisphere.

Nicknamed the 'solar' web for its sunburst of radiating nerve fibers, this abdominal structure sits behind the stomach and in front of the diaphragm's crura, near where several major arteries branch off the aorta — what is it?
Celiac plexus: Complex network of nerves located in the upper abdomen.
Discovered entirely by accident and marketed as Librium, this 1960-approved medication was the first benzodiazepine ever synthesized — what is it?
Chlordiazepoxide: Benzodiazepine medication. Chlordiazepoxide hydrochloride, sold under the brand name Librium, is a sedative and hypnotic medication of the benzodiazepine class.
Home to jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones, this phylum of aquatic invertebrates is defined by specialized stinging cells used to capture prey — what is it?
Cnidaria: Aquatic animal phylum having cnidocytes.

This physician was convicted of involuntary manslaughter in 2011 after inadvertently overdosing his famous patient with the anesthetic propofol, which he had been improperly using as a sleep aid — who is he?
Conrad Murray: American physician and convicted felon (born 1953)
Native to the Andes and Mesoamerica, this plant genus includes five edible species known variously as squash, pumpkin or gourd — which genus?
In psychiatry, this is a fixed false belief that persists even in the face of clear contradicting evidence, commonly seen in schizophrenia and manic episodes of bipolar disorder — what is it?
Delusion: Fixation of holding false beliefs.
Spanning some 40 species from oceanic to river-dwelling and ranging down to a human-sized 1.7 meters, these toothed whales are kin to belugas and porpoises — what are they?
Dolphin: Informal classification of marine mammals, closely related to whales and porpoises.
Credited as the first to create a transuranium element — neptunium — this Berkeley physicist shared the 1951 Nobel in Chemistry with Glenn Seaborg. Who was he?
Also called Human Factors Engineering, this discipline applies psychology and physiology to reduce errors and boost safety in system design — what field?
Ergonomics: Designing systems to suit their users.
One of only two living species in its genus, this rodent was such a prized delicacy to the ancient Romans that its common name literally advertises the fact. What animal is it?
European edible dormouse: Species of rodent.
Known as the weeping fig and the official tree of Bangkok, this flowering plant native to Asia and Australia is often used as a biomonitor in cities — which species?
Ficus benjamina: Species of fig. The species is also naturalized in the West Indies and in the states of Florida and Arizona in the United States.
Working in Feynman's group on the Manhattan Project before co-detecting an elusive elementary particle with Clyde Cowan, he won the 1995 Nobel for catching the neutrino — who was he?
This field studies how geography shapes international relations and foreign policy, though critics have dismissed its early theories as pseudoscience — which discipline?
Geopolitics: Study of geography's effects on politics.
Known online by the alias 'anakata,' this Swedish computer specialist co-founded a notorious BitTorrent site and later helped WikiLeaks with its 2010 release of a leaked military video — who is he?
Gottfrid Svartholm: Swedish computer specialist. Parts of an interview with Svartholm commenting on the May 2006 police raid of The Pirate Bay are featured in Good Copy Bad Copy and Steal This Film.
This protein filament that grows from follicles in the skin is one of the defining traits of mammals, and its removal or styling carries different meanings across cultures — what is it?
Hair: Protein filament that grows from follicles found in the dermis, or skin.
This field of study focuses on the methodological principles of interpreting texts — especially biblical and philosophical writings — and is closely related to exegesis. What is it called?
Hermeneutics: The study of the methodological principles of interpretation. As necessary, hermeneutics may include the art of understanding and communication.
In Greek myth, this fragrant spring bulb sprang from the blood of a youth slain by a jealous west wind god who coveted his bond with Apollo — what flower is it?
Powered by four underperforming Lyulka turbojets, this aircraft became the first Soviet jet bomber to fly before being cancelled in September 1947 — which plane?
Ilyushin Il-22: 1947 Soviet bomber aircraft prototype. The Ilyushin Il-22, USAF/DOD designation Type 10, was the first Soviet jet-engined bomber to fly.
The biggest cat in the Americas, it has a bite so powerful it can crack a turtle's shell or punch straight through a skull between the ears — which animal?
Jaguar: Large cat native to the Americas.
This New Zealand-American sexologist at Johns Hopkins coined the very phrases 'gender role' and 'sexual orientation' — which controversial researcher is it?
John Money: New Zealand psychologist and sexologist (1921–2006)

He coauthored the classic 1973 textbook Gravitation, advised Carl Sagan on wormholes for the novel Contact, and shared the 2017 Nobel Prize for the LIGO detection of gravitational waves — which astrophysicist?
Kip Thorne: American physicist, writer, and Nobel Laureate (born 1940)

Named from the Greek word for 'honey bee' because its flowers attract them, this citrus-scented herb in the mint family has been cultivated since at least the 16th century for tea and aromatic oils — what is it?
This four-engine American turboprop can land on dirt strips and unprepared runways, then moonlight as a gunship, a flying firefighter, or a weather scout — which versatile workhorse is it?
Lockheed C-130 Hercules: American military transport aircraft.

With a fruiting body resembling an open umbrella, this fungus often grows in fairy rings across Eurasian pastures and is prized as a good edible despite resembling toxic look-alikes — what's its scientific name?
Macrolepiota procera: Species of fungus. Macrolepiota procera, the parasol mushroom, is a basidiomycete fungus with a large, prominent fruiting body resembling a parasol.
A Zainichi Korean entrepreneur, this founder and CEO of SoftBank turned a $20 million bet on Alibaba in 2000 into a stake worth around $75 billion — who is he?
In medicine, this term describes a disease spreading from a primary site to a secondary one — most often used for a cancer seeding new tumors elsewhere in the body — what is it?
Metastasis: Spreading of a disease inside a body. The newly pathological sites, then, are metastases (mets).
Medically termed a 'spontaneous abortion,' this is the loss of an embryo or fetus before it can survive independently — distinct from a stillbirth, which occurs after 20 weeks. What is it?
Miscarriage: Natural premature termination of pregnancy.
Native to the Americas from Texas down to Argentina, this domesticated waterfowl species has also gone feral in New Zealand, Australia, and parts of Europe — which species?
Muscovy duck: Species of bird. The Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) is a species of duck native to the Americas, from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas and Mexico south to Argentina and Uruguay.
A cable-like bundle of axons wrapped in three layers of connective tissue, this structure carries electrochemical signals called action potentials — what is it?
Nerve: Cable-like bundle of axons. The axons are bundled together into groups called fascicles, and each fascicle is wrapped in a layer of connective tissue called the perineurium.
This burrowing, semiaquatic South American rodent munches river-plant stems and was shipped worldwide by fur farmers, only to become a destructive invasive pest — which animal is it?
Nutria: Semi-aquatic rodent from South America.
In young children it can mean ear-pulling, extra crying, and poor sleep; it's a group of inflammatory diseases of the middle ear, from acute infections to lingering fluid. What's the medical name?
Otitis media: Inflammation of the middle ear. One of the two main types is acute otitis media (AOM), an infection of rapid onset that usually presents with ear pain.
Found in mice, cats, birds, humans, and dogs but absent in whales and most reptiles, this triangular bone is the body's largest sesamoid — what is it?
Patella: Kneecap, bone covering knee joint.
Found naturally in chocolate — especially after fermentation — this trace amine stimulates the central nervous system by binding to a receptor called TAAR1. What compound is it?
Phenethylamine: Organic compound, a stimulant in humans.

Often at its worst with the very first steps of the day, this common foot disorder inflames the connective tissue supporting the arch and is linked to tight calf muscles and heel spurs — what condition is it?

Plantar fasciitis: Connective tissue disorder of the heel. Plantar fasciitis or plantar heel pain is a disorder of the plantar fascia, which is the connective tissue that supports the arch of the foot.
Sold under the brand name Lyrica, this anticonvulsant amino-acid drug also treats fibromyalgia, nerve pain, and anxiety — which medication is it?
Pregabalin: Anticonvulsant medication. Its use in epilepsy is as an add-on therapy for partial seizures.
This water-soluble organic compound, made of two fused rings, gives its name to a class that includes DNA's adenine and guanine bases — what is it?
Named for the way light stretches toward longer wavelengths, this phenomenon comes in Doppler, gravitational, and cosmological forms and is measured by the value z — what is it?
Redshift: Change in wavelength of light.
Grown in South Africa's Fynbos biome, this caffeine-free herbal infusion has an earthy flavor similar to yerba mate and carries protected designation of origin status in the EU. What is it?
Rooibos: Species of plant in the family Fabaceae.

This Harvard political scientist coordinated security planning for Jimmy Carter's National Security Council, but he's best remembered for a 1993 theory arguing future wars would be fought between cultures rather than countries — who was he?
Samuel P. Huntington: American political scientist and academic (1927–2008)
Born in Moscow and brought to the US at age six, this computer scientist co-founded Google with Larry Page and served as president of its parent company until 2019 — who is he?
Native to the Arctic tundra, this large white bird of prey is famous for being the only member of its family with predominantly pale plumage — which bird?
Snowy owl: Species of owl. The snowy owl (Bubo scandiacus), also known as the polar owl, the white owl and the Arctic owl, is a large, white owl of the true owl family.
This Polish-American mathematician on the Manhattan Project dreamed up the cellular automaton and the Monte Carlo method, and co-designed the thermonuclear bomb — who was he?
Stanisław Ulam: Polish mathematician and physicist (1909–1984)
Comprising around 90 species split between river martins and all other members, this family of aerial-feeding songbirds is thought to have evolved as hole-nesters in Africa — what are they called?
Swallow: Family of songbirds. The term "swallow" is used as the common name for Hirundo rustica in the United Kingdom and Ireland.
Made of collagen like its bone-to-bone cousin the ligament, this tough band of connective tissue instead links muscle to bone, and there are about 4,000 of them in your body — what is it called?
Tendon: Type of tissue that connects muscle to bone.
Native to Africa and the Middle East, this freshwater fish has become a global aquaculture staple but can turn invasive in warm habitats like Australia — which fish?
Tilapia: Common name for many species of fish.
This essential amino acid, which the body can't make on its own, is a precursor to serotonin, melatonin, and vitamin B3 — which amino acid?

Discovered in 1801 by a Spanish-Mexican scientist but only confirmed as a new element in 1830, this hard silvery-grey transition metal takes its name from a Scandinavian goddess of beauty — what element is it?
Vanadium: Chemical element with atomic number 23 (V)
Recognized by their unusually long snouts, these small herbivorous beetles number around 97,000 species and include notorious crop pests that damage stored grain — what are they called?
Weevil: Superfamily of beetles. It also includes bark beetles, which while morphologically dissimilar to other weevils in lacking the distinctive snout, is a subfamily of Curculionidae.

Ranging from small shrubs to tree-like giants such as the Joshua tree, this North American desert plant genus relies on a specialized moth for pollination and is also called Adam's needle — what genus is it?
Yucca: Plant genus in the agave subfamily.
